## Overview

The first notebook of this folder shows how the density of the *spine* age $A^*$
responds to constant, linear and piecewise-linear rates.
This one repeats the exercise for three smoother families of rate:
piecewise-exponential rates (linear on the log scale),
quadratic and quadratic-spline rates,
and sinusoidal rates.
Conditional on at least one individual being alive at $T$,
the spine age has a density on $(0,T)$ and an atom at $a=T$.

The notation is that of `01_spine_age_shapes.qmd`:
$\gamma=\lambda-\mu$,
$\Lambda(s,e]=\int_s^e\lambda$,
$M(s,e]=\int_s^e\mu$,
$\Gamma(s,e]=\Lambda(s,e]-M(s,e]$,
$\mathcal W(b)=e^{\Gamma(0,b]}+\int_0^b\mu(t)\,e^{\Gamma(t,b]}\,dt$
and $\pi(b)=1/\mathcal W(b)$.
With $L_\mu(s,T)=\int_s^T\mu(t)\,e^{\Gamma(t,T]}\,dt$,
the spine density is

$$
  \Pr(A^*\in da)=\lambda(T-a)\,e^{-\Lambda(T-a,T]}\,L_\mu(T-a,T)\,da,
  \qquad
  \Pr(A^*=T)=\mathcal W(T)\,e^{-\Lambda(0,T]}.
$$

Age and calendar time are mirrored, $a=T-\tau$,
so a feature of a rate at calendar time $\tau$ shows up in the density at age $T-\tau$.
Each panel below has the rates $\lambda(\tau)$ and $\mu(\tau)$ against calendar time on top
and the spine density against age underneath.
The atom at $a=T$ is drawn as a point on a stem;
its height is a probability mass, not a density.

## Setup

```{python}
# ruff: noqa: E402
# bdpinf must be imported before jax so its JAX_PLATFORMS=cpu default
# (see src/bdpinf/__init__.py) takes effect before jax reads the env var.
from functools import partial

import jax.numpy as jnp
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
from IPython.display import display
from scipy.integrate import quad

from bdpinf import find_project_root
from bdpinf.models import (
    PiecewiseExponentialRate,
    PiecewiseQuadraticRate,
    SinusoidalRate,
)
from bdpinf.models.math_age_densities import (
    non_spine_age_cdf,
    spine_age_cdf,
    spine_age_log_atom,
    spine_age_log_density,
)
from bdpinf.models.rate_functions import (
    PiecewiseConstantRate,
    PiecewiseLinearRate,
    RateFunction,
)
from bdpinf.visualization import save_chart, scenario_row

figures_dir = find_project_root() / "figures" / "validation" / "time_varying_rates"
figures_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

T = 3.0
AGES = jnp.linspace(1e-3, T - 1e-3, 400)
TIMES = jnp.array([T])
```

```{python}
Scenario = tuple[RateFunction, RateFunction]

# Every scenario drawn below is registered here for the numerical checks.
registry: dict[str, Scenario] = {}


def const(value: float) -> PiecewiseConstantRate:
    """Constant rate ``value`` on ``[0, T]``."""
    return PiecewiseConstantRate.constant(value, T)


def line(start: float, end: float) -> PiecewiseLinearRate:
    """Linear rate from ``start`` at 0 to ``end`` at T."""
    return PiecewiseLinearRate.continuous(jnp.array([start, end]), TIMES)


def exponential(*knots: float, epochs: jnp.ndarray = TIMES) -> PiecewiseExponentialRate:
    """Continuous piecewise-exponential rate through ``knots``."""
    return PiecewiseExponentialRate.continuous(jnp.array(knots), epochs)


def sine(
    mean: float, amplitude: float, period: float, phase: float = 0.0
) -> SinusoidalRate:
    """Sinusoidal rate on ``[0, T]``."""
    return SinusoidalRate(mean, amplitude, period, phase, end_time=T)


def spine_figure(scenarios: dict[str, Scenario], slug: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Register, draw and save a row of spine-density panels; return its summary."""
    registry.update(scenarios)
    fig = partial(scenario_row, primary="spine", show_secondary=False, ages=AGES)(
        scenarios
    )
    display(fig)
    save_chart(fig, slug, output_dir=figures_dir)
    return shape_summary(scenarios)


def shape_summary(scenarios: dict[str, Scenario]) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Mode and height of the spine density on the grid, and the atom mass."""
    rows = []
    for name, (lam, mu) in scenarios.items():
        density = np.exp(np.asarray(spine_age_log_density(AGES, lam, mu)))
        rows.append(
            {
                "scenario": name,
                "mode age": float(AGES[np.argmax(density)]),
                "peak density": float(density.max()),
                "density at a=T": float(density[-1]),
                "local maxima": int(
                    np.sum(
                        (density[1:-1] > density[:-2]) & (density[1:-1] > density[2:])
                    )
                ),
                "atom mass": float(jnp.exp(spine_age_log_atom(lam, mu))),
            }
        )
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)
```

In every table below,
"mode age", "peak density", "density at a=T" and "local maxima" refer to the continuous part of the density on the plotting grid,
and "atom mass" is $\Pr(A^*=T)$.

## Piecewise-exponential birth rate

A piecewise-exponential rate is linear on the log scale within each epoch:
on an epoch of length $d$ with end values $v_0$ and $v_1$ it is $v_0(v_1/v_0)^{(t-t_0)/d}$.
It is positive, and continuous when the end value of one epoch is the start value of the next.
Here the death rate is constant, $\mu=0.7$,
and only $\lambda$ changes.
With one epoch, the exponential rate and the linear rate with the same end points
differ only in the interpolation between the end points.

```{python}
MU_FIXED = 0.7
EXP_ONE_EPOCH = {"rising": (0.3, 1.8), "falling": (1.8, 0.3)}

exp_one = {}
for shape, (start, end) in EXP_ONE_EPOCH.items():
    exp_one[f"λ {shape}, exponential"] = (exponential(start, end), const(MU_FIXED))
    exp_one[f"λ {shape}, linear"] = (line(start, end), const(MU_FIXED))

summary_exp_one = spine_figure(exp_one, "vtv04_exponential_one_epoch")
display(summary_exp_one)
```

In all four panels the density is zero at $a=0$ and has a single maximum.
With a rising $\lambda$ the mode is at a young age (0.70 for the exponential rate, 0.77 for the linear rate) and the atom is large (0.426 and 0.356).
With a falling $\lambda$ the mode is at an older age (2.14 and 1.65) and the atom is smaller (0.272 and 0.234).
For the same end points the exponential rate lies below the straight line between them,
and the tables show what that does:
the mode moves by about 0.5 in age (falling case) and the atom by about 0.07 in mass (rising case).

Two epochs, continuous at the knot $\tau=1.5$,
give a hump (rise then fall) and a dip (fall then rise) in $\lambda$:

```{python}
EXP_TWO_EPOCHS = jnp.array([1.5, T])
EXP_TWO_KNOTS = {"hump": (0.3, 1.8, 0.3), "dip": (1.8, 0.3, 1.8)}

exp_two = {
    f"λ {shape}, exponential": (
        exponential(*knots, epochs=EXP_TWO_EPOCHS),
        const(MU_FIXED),
    )
    for shape, knots in EXP_TWO_KNOTS.items()
}

summary_exp_two = spine_figure(exp_two, "vtv04_exponential_two_epochs")
display(summary_exp_two)
```

The kink of $\lambda$ at $\tau=1.5$ is a kink of the density at $a=T-1.5=1.5$.
For the hump the density has a cusp-shaped peak there (height 0.501 at age 1.50) and falls steeply at older ages.
For the dip the density has a local minimum at the kink and two local maxima, a low one at a young age and the higher one near the oldest ages (mode 2.89, density 0.379 at $a=T$),
so the continuous part of the density does not drop towards $a=T$.

## Quadratic and quadratic-spline birth rate

A quadratic rate is specified by its values at the start, midpoint and end of each epoch.
With one epoch this gives a concave hump or a convex dip,
and the constructor checks that the rate stays non-negative on $[0,T]$.
With several epochs, `PiecewiseQuadraticRate.spline` builds the $C^1$ quadratic spline through chosen knot values:
the rate and its slope are continuous at the knots,
and only the slope at time $0$ is free.
As a comparison, the continuous piecewise-linear rate through the same knot values is drawn next to each spline.
The death rate is again constant, $\mu=0.7$.

```{python}
QUAD_ONE_EPOCH = {
    "hump": (0.3, 1.7, 0.3),
    "dip": (1.5, 0.3, 1.5),
    "skewed hump": (0.3, 1.5, 0.6),
}

quad_one = {}
for shape, (start, mid, end) in QUAD_ONE_EPOCH.items():
    quadratic = PiecewiseQuadraticRate(
        jnp.array([start]), jnp.array([mid]), jnp.array([end]), TIMES
    )
    assert float(jnp.min(quadratic(AGES))) >= 0.0, shape
    quad_one[f"λ quadratic {shape}"] = (quadratic, const(MU_FIXED))

summary_quad_one = spine_figure(quad_one, "vtv04_quadratic_one_epoch")
display(summary_quad_one)
```

The concave hump gives one mode, at age 1.08 (peak density 0.416), and the smallest atom of the three (0.262).
That mode is younger than the mirror image of the peak of $\lambda$, which is at $a=1.5$.
The skewed hump, whose $\lambda$ peaks slightly after the middle of $[0,T]$ and ends higher than it starts, has a similar single mode (age 1.07, peak 0.386).
The convex dip has two local maxima, the higher at age 2.95, and the largest atom (0.383):
the high birth rate near $\tau=0$ is mirrored at ages near $T$.

```{python}
SPLINE_EPOCHS = jnp.array([1.5, T])
SPLINE_SHAPES = {
    # name: (knot values at 0, 1.5 and T, slope at time 0)
    "hump": ((0.5, 1.5, 0.5), 0.0),
    "dip": ((1.2, 0.4, 1.2), -0.8),
}

RATE_GRID = jnp.linspace(0.0, T, 601)
spline_scenarios = {}
spline_extremes = []
for shape, (knots, slope0) in SPLINE_SHAPES.items():
    spline = PiecewiseQuadraticRate.spline(jnp.array(knots), slope0, SPLINE_EPOCHS)
    knotted_line = PiecewiseLinearRate.continuous(jnp.array(knots), SPLINE_EPOCHS)
    assert float(jnp.min(spline(AGES))) >= 0.0, shape
    spline_scenarios[f"λ spline {shape}"] = (spline, const(MU_FIXED))
    spline_extremes.append(
        {
            "shape": shape,
            "knot values": knots,
            "spline min": float(jnp.min(spline(RATE_GRID))),
            "spline max": float(jnp.max(spline(RATE_GRID))),
            "time of extreme": float(
                RATE_GRID[
                    jnp.argmax(spline(RATE_GRID))
                    if shape == "hump"
                    else jnp.argmin(spline(RATE_GRID))
                ]
            ),
        }
    )
    spline_scenarios[f"λ linear {shape}"] = (knotted_line, const(MU_FIXED))

summary_spline = spine_figure(spline_scenarios, "vtv04_quadratic_spline_two_epochs")
display(summary_spline)
display(pd.DataFrame(spline_extremes).round(3))
```

The spline is smooth at $\tau=1.5$, so its density has no kink at $a=1.5$,
while the piecewise-linear rate through the same knots gives a kink there.
The table of extremes shows that the spline does not stay between its knot values:
in the hump it rises above the middle knot (maximum 1.83 against 1.5) and in the dip it falls below it (minimum 0.37 against 0.4).
The densities differ accordingly.
For the hump the spline gives a mode at age 0.87 and peak 0.422, against 1.38 and 0.395 for the linear rate.
For the dip both densities have two local maxima, with the later one higher (mode 2.77, peak 0.319 for the spline; 2.53 and 0.291 for the linear rate), and the atom is 0.382 against 0.344.

## Sinusoidal rates

A sinusoidal rate is $m+A\sin(2\pi\tau/P+\varphi)$
with mean $m\ge|A|$, amplitude $A$, period $P$ and phase $\varphi$.
Its mean over a whole number of periods is $m$,
so changing $P$ at fixed $m$ and $A$ changes how the births (or deaths) are spread over calendar time
and not their average level.
With $T=3$, a period of $P=3$ is one oscillation on $[0,T]$ and $P=0.5$ is six.

### Sinusoidal birth rate, constant death rate

```{python}
SINE_BIRTH = {  # name: (mean, amplitude, period)
    "P=3": (1.0, 0.8, 3.0),
    "P=1": (1.0, 0.8, 1.0),
    "P=0.5": (1.0, 0.8, 0.5),
    "P=1, small amplitude": (1.0, 0.3, 1.0),
}

sine_birth = {
    f"λ sine, {name}": (sine(*params), const(MU_FIXED))
    for name, params in SINE_BIRTH.items()
}

summary_sine_birth = spine_figure(sine_birth, "vtv04_sinusoidal_birth")
display(summary_sine_birth)
```

The density oscillates with the birth rate, at the mirrored ages.
Its number of local maxima is 2, 4 and 7 for $P=3$, $1$ and $0.5$,
which is one more than the number of oscillations of $\lambda$ on $[0,T]$ (1, 3 and 6);
the extra one is a small bump at young ages.
The peak density barely changes with the period (0.520, 0.514, 0.543),
and the atom grows a little as the period shortens (0.243, 0.272, 0.282).
Reducing the amplitude from 0.8 to 0.3 at $P=1$ lowers the peak to 0.368 and flattens the oscillations.

### Constant birth rate, sinusoidal death rate

```{python}
LAMBDA_FIXED = 1.0
SINE_DEATH = {  # name: (mean, amplitude, period)
    "P=3": (0.8, 0.6, 3.0),
    "P=1": (0.8, 0.6, 1.0),
    "P=0.5": (0.8, 0.6, 0.5),
}

sine_death = {
    f"μ sine, {name}": (const(LAMBDA_FIXED), sine(*params))
    for name, params in SINE_DEATH.items()
}

summary_sine_death = spine_figure(sine_death, "vtv04_sinusoidal_death")
display(summary_sine_death)
```

The oscillations are much weaker than for a sinusoidal birth rate:
the density is a broad hump with ripples whose number grows as the period shrinks
(2, 2 and 4 local maxima for $P=3$, $1$ and $0.5$).
In the density formula only $\lambda$ enters as a pointwise factor, which is consistent with this.
The slowest oscillation ($P=3$) has the oldest mode (age 2.21) and the largest atom (0.327),
while $P=1$ and $0.5$ put the mode at about age 1.

### Sinusoidal birth and death rates with different periods

```{python}
SINE_BOTH = {  # name: (birth (mean, amplitude, period, phase), death (...))
    "P=1 and 1.5": ((1.0, 0.7, 1.0, 0.0), (0.8, 0.5, 1.5, 0.0)),
    "P=0.5 and 1.25": ((1.0, 0.7, 0.5, 0.0), (0.8, 0.5, 1.25, 0.0)),
    "P=3 and 0.6, μ phase π": ((1.0, 0.7, 3.0, 0.0), (0.8, 0.5, 0.6, float(np.pi))),
}

sine_both = {
    f"λ, μ sine, {name}": (sine(*birth), sine(*death))
    for name, (birth, death) in SINE_BOTH.items()
}

summary_sine_both = spine_figure(sine_both, "vtv04_sinusoidal_both")
display(summary_sine_both)
```

With birth period 1 and death period 1.5 the density oscillates at the birth period (local maxima near ages 0.8, 1.7 and 2.7 in the figure),
with the highest peak in the notebook (0.576 at age 1.68).
With birth period 0.5 and death period 1.25 the density has six local maxima, the first four of similar height
and the last two lower, towards $a=T$.
With a slow birth rate ($P=3$) and a fast death rate ($P=0.6$, phase $\pi$),
the density follows the slow birth rate, with a broad flat top between ages of about 1.5 and 2,
a small bump at young ages, and the smallest atom of the notebook (0.204).

## Numerical checks

Three checks support the figures above, over every scenario drawn in this notebook.
Each check has an `assert`, so rendering fails if one fails.

1. Total mass: the spine CDF at $T$ (including the atom) and the non-spine CDF at $T$ both equal 1.
2. An independent oracle for a few scenarios: the spine density equals
   $\lambda(T-a)\,e^{-\Lambda(T-a,T]}\,L_\mu(T-a,T)$,
   with $L_\mu$ computed by adaptive quadrature (`scipy.integrate.quad`)
   from the rates' own `integral` for $\Lambda$ and $\Gamma$,
   a different code path from the Gauss--Legendre segments used by the library.
3. Consistency with the existing families:
   an exponential rate with equal end values is a constant rate,
   and a quadratic rate with zero curvature is a linear rate.

```{python}
end = jnp.array([T])
MASS_ATOL = 1e-8
mass_table = pd.DataFrame(
    {
        "scenario": list(registry),
        "spine mass": [float(spine_age_cdf(end, *v)[0]) for v in registry.values()],
        "non-spine mass": [
            float(non_spine_age_cdf(end, *v)[0]) for v in registry.values()
        ],
    }
)
mass_table["max |error|"] = np.maximum(
    np.abs(mass_table["spine mass"] - 1.0), np.abs(mass_table["non-spine mass"] - 1.0)
)
display(mass_table)
assert (mass_table["max |error|"] < MASS_ATOL).all()
largest_mass_error = mass_table["max |error|"].max()
print(f"{len(mass_table)} scenarios, largest mass error {largest_mass_error:.2e}")
```

```{python}
ORACLE_AGES = (0.4, 1.3, 2.5)
ORACLE_RTOL = 1e-8
ORACLE_SCENARIOS = [
    "λ rising, exponential",
    "λ hump, exponential",
    "λ quadratic hump",
    "λ spline hump",
    "λ spline dip",
    "λ sine, P=0.5",
    "μ sine, P=1",
    "λ, μ sine, P=0.5 and 1.25",
]


def oracle_spine_density(lam: RateFunction, mu: RateFunction, age: float) -> float:
    """lambda(T-a) exp(-Lambda(T-a,T)) L_mu(T-a,T), with L_mu by adaptive quadrature."""
    s = T - age

    def integrand(t: float) -> float:
        gamma_t = float(
            lam.integral(jnp.array(t), jnp.array(T))
            - mu.integral(jnp.array(t), jnp.array(T))
        )
        return float(mu(jnp.array(t))) * np.exp(gamma_t)

    kinks = {
        float(b)
        for rate in (lam, mu)
        for b in np.asarray(rate.breakpoints)
        if s < b < T
    }
    l_mu, _ = quad(
        integrand,
        s,
        T,
        points=sorted(kinks) or None,
        epsabs=0.0,
        epsrel=1e-13,
        limit=400,
    )
    big_lambda = float(lam.integral(jnp.array(s), jnp.array(T)))
    return float(lam(jnp.array(s))) * np.exp(-big_lambda) * l_mu


oracle_rows = []
for name in ORACLE_SCENARIOS:
    lam, mu = registry[name]
    library = np.exp(np.asarray(spine_age_log_density(jnp.array(ORACLE_AGES), lam, mu)))
    for age, value in zip(ORACLE_AGES, library, strict=True):
        expected = oracle_spine_density(lam, mu, age)
        oracle_rows.append(
            {
                "scenario": name,
                "age": age,
                "bdpinf": float(value),
                "quadrature oracle": expected,
                "relative error": abs(float(value) - expected) / abs(expected),
            }
        )
oracle_table = pd.DataFrame(oracle_rows)
display(oracle_table)
assert (oracle_table["relative error"] < ORACLE_RTOL).all()
print(f"largest oracle relative error {oracle_table['relative error'].max():.2e}")
```

```{python}
CONSISTENCY_ATOL = 1e-10
CONSTANT_VALUE = 1.3
TWO_EPOCHS = jnp.array([1.5, T])
LINEAR_ENDS = {  # name: (start values, end values, epoch end times)
    "one epoch": (jnp.array([0.3]), jnp.array([1.8]), TIMES),
    "two epochs, with a jump": (
        jnp.array([0.4, 1.2]),
        jnp.array([1.6, 0.5]),
        TWO_EPOCHS,
    ),
}

mu_ref = const(MU_FIXED)
pairs: dict[str, tuple[Scenario, Scenario]] = {
    "exponential, equal end values, vs constant": (
        (
            PiecewiseExponentialRate.continuous(
                jnp.array([CONSTANT_VALUE, CONSTANT_VALUE]), TIMES
            ),
            mu_ref,
        ),
        (const(CONSTANT_VALUE), mu_ref),
    ),
    "exponential death rate, equal end values, vs constant": (
        (
            const(CONSTANT_VALUE),
            PiecewiseExponentialRate.from_constant(jnp.array([0.7]), TIMES),
        ),
        (const(CONSTANT_VALUE), mu_ref),
    ),
}
for name, (v0, v1, times) in LINEAR_ENDS.items():
    pairs[f"quadratic from_linear vs linear, {name}"] = (
        (PiecewiseQuadraticRate.from_linear(v0, v1, times), mu_ref),
        (PiecewiseLinearRate(v0, v1, times), mu_ref),
    )

consistency_rows = []
for name, (new, old) in pairs.items():
    dens_new = np.exp(np.asarray(spine_age_log_density(AGES, *new)))
    dens_old = np.exp(np.asarray(spine_age_log_density(AGES, *old)))
    atom_new = float(jnp.exp(spine_age_log_atom(*new)))
    atom_old = float(jnp.exp(spine_age_log_atom(*old)))
    consistency_rows.append(
        {
            "comparison": name,
            "max density difference": float(np.max(np.abs(dens_new - dens_old))),
            "atom difference": abs(atom_new - atom_old),
        }
    )
consistency_table = pd.DataFrame(consistency_rows)
display(consistency_table)
assert (consistency_table["max density difference"] < CONSISTENCY_ATOL).all()
assert (consistency_table["atom difference"] < CONSISTENCY_ATOL).all()
```
